lesson.title: Joining Lists End to End: List Concatenation with +
lesson.summary: The + operator joins two lists into a new list without changing either original, the same way + joins two strings, while += and append() offer related but distinctly different behavior worth telling apart.
lesson.body:
You already know that + joins two strings together into a new, longer string, leaving the original strings untouched. Lists support the exact same operator with the exact same spirit: original_list + other_list produces a brand new list containing every element of the first list followed by every element of the second, and neither original list is changed in the process.

```python
morning = ["cereal", "toast"]
afternoon = ["sandwich", "soup"]
menu = morning + afternoon
print(menu)
print(morning)
```

This prints:

```
['cereal', 'toast', 'sandwich', 'soup']
['cereal', 'toast']
```

menu is an entirely new list built out of the elements of both, and morning still holds only its original two items afterward, exactly as string concatenation leaves its original strings alone. Just like string concatenation, both sides of + have to be the same type, so list + list works but list + a single number or list + a string will raise a TypeError, since Python has no idea whether you meant to add a single new element or something else entirely.

The += operator does something related but worth telling apart carefully. On a list, += extends the list in place with the elements of whatever follows, rather than building a separate new list the way plain + does.

```python
totals = [10, 20]
totals += [30, 40]
print(totals)

totals.append([50, 60])
print(totals)
```

This prints:

```
[10, 20, 30, 40]
[10, 20, 30, 40, [50, 60]]
```

totals += [30, 40] merges the two lists together, adding 30 and 40 as their own individual elements, which is concatenation. But totals.append([50, 60]) does something different on purpose: append() always adds its argument as a single element, so the whole list [50, 60] gets tucked in as one nested item at the end, rather than being merged in as two separate numbers. That distinction, merging elements together versus nesting a whole list as one element, is exactly the difference between concatenation and the append() behavior you saw back when nested lists were introduced, and mixing the two up is one of the most common sources of unexpectedly nested data in real programs.
